idiom_name: IntRange / LongRange / CharRange with contains ('in') and coerceIn
implementation_notes: kotlin.ranges puts ranges into the standard library: 1..10 is a closed IntRange, 1 until 10 is half-open, `in` dispatches to contains, and coerceIn/coerceAtLeast clamp a value into a range. Over an arbitrary Comparable, a..b yields a ClosedRange<T> with the same membership operator, which is how a LocalDate period is usually modelled. What the stdlib does not supply is interval-to-interval logic (no overlap, intersection or span) and open-ended ranges: Kotlin ranges are always bounded on both sides, so 'from x onwards' is expressed as a nullable endpoint in the domain type, and overlap is a two-comparison helper.
code_sketch:
val window = 1..10                       // IntRange, closed
val slot = 1.until(10)                   // half-open [1, 10)
val letter = 'a'..'z'

val period = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1)..LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 31)  // ClosedRange<LocalDate>

fun <T : Comparable<T>> overlaps(a: ClosedRange<T>, b: ClosedRange<T>) =
    a.start <= b.endInclusive && b.start <= a.endInclusive
pitfalls: Kotlin ranges are also iterables, which invites looping over an interval where a containment test was meant; and a ClosedRange over a non-iterable domain (LocalDate) simply is not iterable, so the two uses diverge by domain.
IntRange.contains is O(1) but a stepped progression (1..10 step 2) is not a ClosedRange in the sense of the comparison helpers, and contains on such a progression falls back to iteration.

There is no stdlib overlap: writing it as a.start <= b.endInclusive && b.start <= a.endInclusive silently treats touching ranges as overlapping, which double-counts the shared endpoint for closed ranges.
Ranges are bounded on both sides, so open-ended periods need own abstraction (nullable endpoints); using Int.MAX_VALUE as 'forever' reintroduces sentinel arithmetic.

variants.name: OpenEndRange and the ..< operator (Kotlin 1.9+)
variants.implementation_notes: Since 1.9 the standard library names the half-open case explicitly: ..< (rangeUntil) produces an OpenEndRange whose endExclusive value is excluded, with contains and isEmpty available, and IntRange/LongRange/CharRange implement both interfaces. Prefer it for time and sequence windows so adjacent intervals do not share an endpoint, and keep ClosedRange where the domain is closed by nature (a period named by its last day). Both interfaces require Comparable, so a custom domain type must implement it before it can be ranged at all.
variants.code_sketch:
val slot: OpenEndRange<Int> = 1..<10           // [1, 10)
val same = 1.rangeUntil(10)                    // named form

val quarter = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1)..<LocalDate.of(2026, 4, 1)
quarter.contains(day)
quarter.isEmpty()
pitfalls: OpenEndRange and ClosedRange are sibling interfaces, not subtypes: a function taking ClosedRange will not accept 1..<10, so public signatures must pick one convention and convert deliberately.

..< requires a Kotlin 1.9+ compiler; on older toolchains the operator does not exist, so half-open intervals are spelled a until b for primitives or by decrementing the closed upper bound - and a decrement is wrong for non-numeric domains.

..< / rangeUntil requires the type to provide a rangeUntil operator: the stdlib defines it for Int, Long, Char and the unsigned primitives, but a custom Comparable domain type does not get it for free, so open-ended intervals over domain types need the operator added or a closed range used instead.
